title: Using Singular Value Decompositions
lead: With the singular value decomposition in hand, this section puts it to work: on least-squares problems, on approximating a matrix by matrices of lower rank, on principal component analysis, on compressing and cleaning up images, and on the voting records of the Supreme Court.
summary_html:
This section has demonstrated some uses of the singular value decomposition. Because the singular values appear in decreasing order, the decomposition has the effect of concentrating the most important features of the matrix into the first singular values and singular vectors.

  • Because the first left singular vectors form an orthonormal basis for $\kCol(\kA)$, a singular value decomposition provides a convenient way to project vectors onto $\kCol(\kA)$ and therefore to solve least-squares problems.
  • A singular value decomposition of a rank $r$ matrix $\kA$ leads to a series of approximations $\kAksub$ of $\kA$ where$$ \begin{aligned} \kA \approx \kAone & = \ksigmaone\kvecuone\kvecvone^T \\ \kA \approx \kAtwo & = \ksigmaone\kvecuone\kvecvone^T + \ksigmatwo\kvecutwo\kvecvtwo^T \\ \kA \approx \kAthree & = \ksigmaone\kvecuone\kvecvone^T + \ksigmatwo\kvecutwo\kvecvtwo^T + \ksigmathree\kvecuthree\kvecvthree^T \\ \vdots & \\ \kA = \kAr & = \ksigmaone\kvecuone\kvecvone^T + \ksigmatwo\kvecutwo\kvecvtwo^T + \ksigmathree\kvecuthree\kvecvthree^T + \ldots + \ksigmar\kvecur\kvecvr^T \end{aligned} $$In each case, $\kAksub$ is the rank $k$ matrix that is closest to $\kA$.
  • If $\kA$ is a demeaned data matrix, the left singular vectors give the principal components of $\kA$, and the variance in the direction of a principal component can be simply expressed in terms of the corresponding singular value.
  • The singular value decomposition has many applications. In this section, we looked at how the decomposition is used in image processing through the techniques of compression and denoising.
  • Because the first few left singular vectors contain the most important features of a matrix, we can use a singular value decomposition to extract meaning from a large dataset as we did when analyzing the voting patterns of the second Rehnquist court.

exercises.prompt:
Suppose that $\kA = \kU\kSigma \kVT$ where

$$ \kSigma = \begin{bmatrix} 13 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 &0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 &0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, $$

vectors $\kvecuj$ form the columns of $\kU$, and vectors $\kvecvj$ form the columns of $\kV$.

  1. What are the shapes of the matrices $\kA$, $\kU$, and $\kV$?

  2. What is the rank of $\kA$?

  3. Describe how to find an orthonormal basis for $\kCol(\kA)$.

  4. Describe how to find an orthonormal basis for $\kNul(\kA)$.

  5. If the columns of $\kQ$ form an orthonormal basis for $\kCol(\kA)$, what is $\kQT\kQ$?

  6. How would you form a matrix that projects vectors orthogonally onto $\kCol(\kA)$?

answer.solution:
1. $\kA$ is $5\times4$, $\kU$ is $5\times5$, and $\kV$ is $4\times4$.

  2. $\operatorname{rank}(\kA)=3$ since there are three nonzero singular values.

  3. The first three columns, $\kvecuone$, $\kvecutwo$, and $\kvecuthree$, of $\kU$ form an orthonormal basis for $\kCol(\kA)$.

  4. The last column $\kvecvfour$ of $\kV$ is a basis for $\kNul(\kA)$.

  5. $\kQT\kQ=\kI$ since each entry is a dot product of two vectors in an orthonormal set.

  6. $\kQ\kQT$ projects vectors orthogonally onto $\kCol(\kA)$.

exercises.prompt:

$$ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \kvecx = \left[\begin{array}{r}-1 \\ 3 \\ 6 \end{array}\right] $$

  1. Find a singular value decomposition for $\kA$ using the Sage cell below. What are singular values of $\kA$?

  2. What is $r$, the rank of $\kA$? How can we identify an orthonormal basis for $\kCol(\kA)$?

Form the reduced singular value decomposition $\kUr\kSigmar\kVr^T$ by constructing: the matrix $\kUr$, consisting of the first $r$ columns of $\kU$; the matrix $\kVr$, consisting of the first $r$ columns of $\kV$; and $\kSigmar$, a square $r\times r$ diagonal matrix. Verify that $\kA=\kUr\kSigmar \kVr^T$.

  4. How does the reduced singular value decomposition provide a matrix whose columns are an orthonormal basis for $\kCol(\kA)$?

  5. Explain why a least-squares approximate solution $\kvecxhat$ satisfies

    $$ \kA\kvecxhat = \kUr\kUr^T\kvecb. $$

  6. What is the product $\kVr\kVr^T$ and why does it have this form?

  7. Explain why

    $$ \kvecxhat = \kVr\kSigmarinv\kUr^T\kvecb $$

    is the least-squares approximate solution, and use this expression to find $\kvecxhat$.

  2. $\operatorname{rank}(\kA) = 2$ and the first two columns of $\kU$ form an orthonormal basis for $\kCol(\kA)$.

  3. We have

    $$ \kUr = \begin{bmatrix} -0.22 & 0.89 \\ -0.52 & 0.25 \\ -0.83 & -0.39 \end{bmatrix},\hspace{24pt} \kSigmar = \begin{bmatrix} 2.7 & 0.00 \\ 0.00 & 0.92 \end{bmatrix},\hspace{24pt} \kVr = \begin{bmatrix} -0.58 & 0.81 \\ -0.81 & -0.58 \end{bmatrix}\text{.} $$

  4. The columns of $\kUr$ form an orthonormal basis for $\kCol(\kA)$.

  5. $\kvecbhat=\kUr\kUr^T\kvecb$

  6. $\kVr^T\kVr = \kI$

  7. $\kvecxhat=\left[\begin{array}{r}-0.83 \\ 3.50 \end{array}\right]$

Solution.

  1. The singular values are $\ksigmaone = 2.67$ and $\ksigmatwo = 0.92$.

  2. There are two nonzero singular values so $\operatorname{rank}(\kA) = 2$. The first two columns of $\kU$ form an orthonormal basis for $\kCol(\kA)$.

  3. We have

    $$ \kUr = \begin{bmatrix} -0.22 & 0.89 \\ -0.52 & 0.25 \\ -0.83 & -0.39 \end{bmatrix},\hspace{24pt} \kSigmar = \begin{bmatrix} 2.7 & 0.00 \\ 0.00 & 0.92 \end{bmatrix},\hspace{24pt} \kVr = \begin{bmatrix} -0.58 & 0.81 \\ -0.81 & -0.58 \end{bmatrix}\text{.} $$

  4. The columns of $\kUr$ form an orthonormal basis for $\kCol(\kA)$.

  5. Since $\kvecbhat=\kUr\kUr^T\kvecb$, we obtain the equation $\kA\kvecxhat = \kUr\kUr^T\kvecb$.

  6. Because the matrix has full rank, we know that $\kNul(\kA)=\{\kveczero\}$. Therefore, $\kVr=\kV$ is a square matrix and $\kVr\kVr^T = \kI$ it is orthogonal.

  7. We have the equation $\kA\kvecxhat = \kUr\kUr^T\kvecb$, which gives

    $$ \begin{aligned} \kA\kvecxhat & = \kUr\kUr^T\kvecb \\ \kUr\kSigmar\kVr^T\kvecxhat & = \kUr\kUr^T\kvecb \\ \kSigmar\kVr^T\kvecxhat & = \kUr^T\kvecb \\ \kVr^T\kvecxhat & = \kSigmarinv\kUr^T\kvecb \\ \kvecxhat & = \kVr\kSigmarinv\kUr^T\kvecb \\ \end{aligned} $$

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. The fraction of the total variance represented by the first two principal components is $97.8\%$.

  2. If $\kvecx = c_1\kvecuone+c_2\kvecutwo+c_3\kvecuthree+c_4\kvecufour$, then $\left[\begin{array}{r}c_1 \\ c_2 \\ c_3 \\ c_4 \end{array}\right]$ is the corresponding column of $\kUT\kA$.

  3. We just need the first two components of the corresponding column of $\kGamma$.

  4. $\left[\begin{array}{r}c_1 \\ c_2 \end{array}\right]$ is the corresponding column of $\kUtwo^T\kA$.

  5. We can construct $\kGammatwo=\kSigmatwo \kVtwo^T$ or just pull out the first two rows of $\kGamma=\kSigma \kVT$.

Solution.

  1. The singular values are $\ksigmaone=25.1$, $\ksigmatwo = 6.0$, $\ksigmathree=3.4$ and $\ksigma_4 = 1.9$. Since $\kVui = \frac{1}{150} \ksigmai^2$, the variances are $4.20$, $0.24$, $0.08$, and $0.02$. The fraction of the total variance represented by the first two principal components is $97.8\%$.

  2. If $\kvecx$ is the $100^{th}$ column of $\kA$, then $\left[\begin{array}{r}c_1 \\ c_2 \\ c_3 \\ c_4 \end{array}\right]$ is the $100^{th}$ column of $\kUT\kA = \kUT(\kU\kSigma \kVT) = \kSigma \kVT = \kGamma$.

  3. The projected data point is $\kvecxhat = c_1\kvecuone + c_2\kvecutwo$ since $c_3\kvecuthree+c_4\kvecufour$ is orthogonal to the subspace spanned by the first two principal components. Therefore, the coordinates of the projected data point are the first two components of the corresponding column of $\kGamma$. The coordinates of all the projected data points are given by the first two rows of $\kGamma$.

  4. Once again, suppose that $\kvecx=c_1\kvecuone+c_2\kvecutwo+c_3\kvecuthree+c_4\kvecufour$ is a column of $\kA$ and that $\kUtwo = \begin{bmatrix}\kvecuone & \kvecutwo \end{bmatrix}$. Then $\left[\begin{array}{r}c_1 \\ c_2 \end{array}\right]$ is the corresponding column of $\kUtwo^T\kA = \kUtwo(\kU\kSigma \kVT) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ \end{bmatrix}\kSigma \kVT = \kSigmatwo \kVtwo^T=\kGammatwo$.

  5. We can construct $\kGammatwo=\kSigmatwo \kVtwo^T$ or just pull out the first two rows of $\kGamma=\kSigma \kVT$.

      $$ \kA = \kAksub = \ksigmaone\kvecuone\kvecvone^T + \ksigmatwo\kvecutwo\kvecvtwo^T + \ldots + \ksigmak\kvecuk\kvecvk^T. $$

exercises.prompt:
Evaluating the following cell loads and displays a dataset describing the votes of each justice in these 911 cases. More specifically, an entry of +1 means that the justice represented by the row voted with the majority in the case represented by the column. An entry of -1 means that justice was in the minority. This information is also stored in the $9\times911$ matrix $\kA$.

sage.repl.load.load('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/davidaustinm/ula_modules/master/svd_supreme.py', globals())
A = matrix(RDF, cases.values)
cases

The justices are listed, very roughly, in order from more conservative to more progressive. In this activity, it will be helpful to visualize the entries in various matrices and vectors. The next cell displays the first 50 columns of the matrix $\kA$ with white representing an entry of +1, red representing -1, and black representing 0.

display_matrix(A.matrix_from_columns(range(50)))

  1. Plot the singular values of $\kA$ below. Describe the significance of this plot, including the relative contributions from the singular values $\ksigmak$ as $k$ increases.

    plot_sv(A)

  2. Form the singular value decomposition $\kA=\kU\kSigma \kVT$ and the matrix of coefficients $\kGamma$ so that $\kA=\kU\kGamma$.

  3. We will now study a particular case, the second case which appears as the column of $\kA$ indexed by 1. There is a command display_column(A, k) that provides a visual display of the $k^{th}$ column of a matrix $\kA$. Describe the justices’ votes in the second case.

  4. Also, display the first left singular vector $\kvecuone$, the column of $\kU$ indexed by $0$, and the column of $\kGamma$ holding the coefficients that express the second case as a linear combination of left singular vectors.

    What does this tell us about how the second case is constructed as a linear combination of left singular vectors? What is the significance of the first left singular vector $\kvecuone$?

  5. Let’s now study the $48^{th}$ case, which is represented by the column of $\kA$ indexed by 47. Describe the voting pattern in this case.

  6. Display the second left singular vector $\kvecutwo$ and the vector of coefficients that express the $48^{th}$ case as a linear combination of left singular vectors.

    Describe how this case is constructed as a linear combination of singular vectors. What is the significance of the second left singular vector $\kvecutwo$?

  7. The data in Table 7.5.2 describes the number of cases decided by each possible vote count.

    How do the singular vectors $\kvecuone$ and $\kvecutwo$ reflect this data? Would you characterize the court as leaning toward the conservatives or progressives? Use these singular vectors to explain your response.

  8. Cases decided by a 5-4 vote are often the most impactful as they represent a sharp divide among the justices and, often, society at large. For that reason, we will now focus on the 5-4 decisions. Evaluating the next cell forms the $9\times188$ matrix $\kB$ consisting of 5-4 decisions.

    B = matrix(RDF, fivefour.values)
display_matrix(B.matrix_from_columns(range(50)))

    Form the singular value decomposition of $\kB=\kU\kSigma \kVT$ along with the matrix $\kGamma$ of coefficients so that $\kB=\kU\kGamma$ and display the first left singular vector $\kvecuone$. Study how the $7^{th}$ case, indexed by 6, is constructed as a linear combination of left singular vectors.

    What does this singular vector tell us about the make up of the court and whether it leans towards the conservatives or progressives?

  9. Display the second left singular vector $\kvecutwo$ and study how the $6^{th}$ case, indexed by 5, is constructed as a linear combination of left singular vectors.

    What does $\kvecutwo$ tell us about the relative importance of the justices’ voting records?

  10. By a swing vote, we mean a justice who is less inclined to vote with a particular bloc of justices but instead swings from one bloc to another with the potential to sway close decisions. What do the singular vectors $\kvecuone$ and $\kvecutwo$ tell us about the presence of voting blocs on the court and the presence of a swing vote? Which justice represents the swing vote?

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. The first two singular values contribute most significantly.

  2. $\kGamma$ is a $9\times911$ matrix that expresses the cases as linear combinations of the left singular vectors.

  3. This is a unanimous decision.

  4. $\kvecuone$ represents a unanimous decision.

  5. This is a 5-4 decision with the 5 conservative justices voting in the majority.

  6. $\kvecutwo$ represents a 5-4 decision.

  7. The most frequently occurring decisions are unanimous and the second most frequently occurring are 5-4.

  8. $\kvecuone$ represents a case where the five conservative justices are voting together.

  9. The second left singular vector $\kvecutwo$ essentially records the vote of Sandra Day O’Connor.

  10. Sandra Day O’Connor

Solution.

  1. The first two singular values contribute most significantly.

  2. $\kGamma$ is a $9\times911$ matrix that expresses the cases as linear combinations of the left singular vectors.

  3. This is a unanimous decision.

  4. The unanimous decision is essentially represented as $-\kvecuone$ so $\kvecuone$ represents a unanimous decision.

  5. This is a 5-4 decision with the 5 conservative justices voting in the majority.

  6. This 5-4 decision is essentially represented as $\kvecutwo$, the second most important left singular vector.

  7. We see that the most decisions are unanimous, which is why $\kvecuone$ represents unanimous decisions. The second most frequently occurring decisions is a 5-4 decision, which is why $\kvecutwo$ represents a 5-4 decision that leans to the conservative justices.

  8. The first singular vector $\kvecuone$ represents a case where the five conservative justices are voting together. From this we conclude that the court leans toward the conservatives.

  9. The second left singular vector $\kvecutwo$ essentially records the vote of Sandra Day O’Connor and shows how her vote has the power to swing a 5-4 decision from a conservative majority to a progressive majority.

  10. Sandra Day O’Connor would be the swing vote.

exercises.prompt:
Suppose that

$$ \kA = \begin{bmatrix} 2.1 & -1.9 & 0.1 & 3.7 \\ -1.5 & 2.7 & 0.9 & -0.6 \\ -0.4 & 2.8 & -1.5 & 4.2 \\ -0.4 & 2.4 & 1.9 & -1.8 \end{bmatrix}\text{.} $$

  1. Find the singular values of $\kA$. What is $\operatorname{rank}(\kA)$?

  2. Find the sequence of matrices $\kAone$, $\kAtwo$, $\kAthree$, and $\kAfour$ where $\kAksub$ is the rank $k$ approximation of $\kA$.

Suppose we would like to find the best quadratic function

$$ \beta_0 + \beta_1x + \beta_2x^2=y $$

fitting the points

$$ (0,1), (1,0), (2,1.5), (3,4), (4,8)\text{.} $$

  1. Set up a linear system $\kA\kvecx = \kvecb$ describing the coefficients $\kvecx = \left[\begin{array}{r}\beta_0 \\ \beta_1 \\ \beta_2 \end{array}\right]$.

  2. Find the singular value decomposition of $\kA$.

  3. Use the singular value decomposition to find the least-squares approximate solution $\kvecxhat$.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. The linear system is

    $$ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 4 \\ 1 & 3 & 9 \\ 1 & 4 & 16 \\ \end{bmatrix} \kvecx = \left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 0 \\ 1.5 \\ 4 \\ 8 \\ \end{array}\right] $$

  2. $\kU$ is a $5\times5$ matrix, $\kSigma$ is $5\times3$, and $\kV$ is $3\times3$

  3. $\kvecxhat=\left[\begin{array}{r}0.87 \\ -1.34 \\ 0.79 \end{array}\right]$

Solution.

  1. The linear system is

    $$ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 4 \\ 1 & 3 & 9 \\ 1 & 4 & 16 \\ \end{bmatrix} \kvecx = \left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 0 \\ 1.5 \\ 4 \\ 8 \\ \end{array}\right] $$

  2. $\kU$ is a $5\times5$ matrix, $\kSigma$ is $5\times3$, and $\kV$ is $3\times3$

  3. The rank of $\kA$ is 3 so we’ll form the reduced singular value decomposition $\kA=\kU_3\kSigma_3\kV_3^T$. Then $\kvecxhat = \kV_3\kSigma_3^{-1}\kU_3^T\kvecb = \left[\begin{array}{r}0.87 \\ -1.34 \\ 0.79 \end{array}\right]$

exercises.prompt:
Remember that the outer product of two vectors $\kvecu$ and $\kvecv$ is the matrix $\kvecu~\kvecv^T$.

  1. Suppose that $\kvecu = \left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ -3 \end{array}\right]$ and $\kvecv=\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$. Evaluate the outer product $\kvecu~\kvecv^T$. To get a clearer sense of how this works, perform this operation without using technology.

    How is each of the columns of $\kvecu~\kvecv^T$ related to $\kvecu$?

  2. Suppose $\kvecu$ and $\kvecv$ are general vectors. What is $\operatorname{rank}(\kvecu~\kvecv^T)$ and what is a basis for its column space $\kCol(\kvecu~\kvecv^T)$?

  3. Suppose that $\kvecu$ is a unit vector. What is the effect of multiplying a vector by the matrix $\kvecu~\kvecu^T$?

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. $\kvecu~\kvecv^T = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 & 2 \\ -6 & 0 & -3 \end{bmatrix}$

  2. The rank is $1$ and $\kvecu$ forms a basis.

  3. This matrix projects vectors orthogonally onto the line defined by $\kvecu$.

Solution.

  1. $\kvecu~\kvecv^T = \begin{bmatrix} 2\kvecu & 0\kvecu & \kvecu \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 & 2 \\ -6 & 0 & -3 \end{bmatrix}$

  2. Since each column of $\kvecu~\kvecv^T$ is a scalar multiple of $\kvecu$, the rank of the matrix is $1$ and $\kvecu$ forms a basis.

  3. This matrix projects vectors orthogonally onto the line defined by $\kvecu$.

exercises.prompt:
Evaluating the following cell loads in a dataset recording some features of 1057 houses. Notice how the lot size varies over a relatively small range compared to the other features. For this reason, in addition to demeaning the data, we’ll scale each feature by dividing by its standard deviation so that the range of values is similar for each feature. The matrix $\kA$ holds the result.

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/davidaustinm/ula_modules/master/data/housing.csv', index_col=0)
df = df.fillna(df.mean())
std = (df-df.mean())/df.std()
A = matrix(std.values).T
df.T

  1. Find the singular values of $\kA$ and use them to determine the variance in the direction of the principal components.

  2. For what fraction of the variance do the first two principal components account?

  3. Find a singular value decomposition of $\kA$ and construct the $2\times1057$ matrix $\kB$ whose entries are the coordinates of the demeaned data points projected on to the two-dimensional subspace spanned by the first two principal components. You can plot the projected data points using list_plot(B.columns()).

  4. Study the entries in the first two principal components $\kvecuone$ and $\kvecutwo$. Would a more expensive house lie on the left, right, top, or bottom of the plot you constructed?

  5. In what ways does a house that lies on the far left of the plot you constructed differ from an average house? In what ways does a house that lies near the top of the plot you constructed differ from an average house?

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. The variances are $1.96$, $1.01$, $0.79$, and $0.24$.

  2. $74\%$

  3. The matrix $\kB$ is formed from the first two rows of the product $\kSigma \kVT$.

  4. Left

  5. Houses on the left have larger living area, lot sizes, and prices and are newer. Houses near the top have larger lot sizes and ages.

Solution.

  1. The singular values $\ksigmai$ are $45.5$, $32.6$, $28.9$, and $15.9$. Therefore, the variances in the direction of the principal components are given by $\frac{1}{1057}\ksigmai^2$ and are $1.96$, $1.01$, $0.79$, and $0.24$.

  2. The first two principal components retain $74\%$ of the total variance.

  3. The matrix $\kB$ is formed from the first two rows of the product $\kSigma \kVT$.

  4. The fourth components, the ones that correspond to house prices, of $\kvecuone$ and $\kvecutwo$ are $-0.65$ and $-0.03$ respectively. This shows us that $\kvecutwo$ doesn’t contribute much to the house price. Moving in the negative $\kvecuone$ direction causes the house price to go up so the more expensive homes are on the left.

  5. The first principal component is $\kvecuone = \left[\begin{array}{r}-0.64 \\ -0.20 \\ 0.36 \\ -0.65 \end{array}\right]$. If we move to the left, this vector is multiplied by a negative number so the living area, lot size, and price go up while the age of the house decreases.

    The second principal component is $\kvecutwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}0.05 \\ 0.86 \\ 0.51 \\ -0.03 \end{array}\right]$. If we move up, this is multiplied by a positive number so the lot size and the age of the house increase.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. For each justice, it tells us the number of times that justice voted with the majority minus the number of times they voted in the minority.

  2. The justice that most often votes with the majority could be a swing vote.

  3. The first five justices usually vote in the majority.

  4. A second justice voted with the majority 84 times more than with the minority.

  5. Anthony Kennedy

Solution.

  1. $\kA\kvecv$ is a 9-dimensional vector. For each justice, it tells us the number of times that justice voted with the majority minus the number of times they voted in the minority.

  2. Out of 188 cases, the fifth justice Sandra Day O’Connor voted with the majority 94 more times than with the minority. Since a swing vote will often vote in the majority, this gives additional evidence that Sandra Day O’Connor is a swing vote.

  3. The first five justices more often vote with the majority and the last four more often with the minority. This means the court leans toward the first five justices, who are the more conservative ones.

  4. The fourth justice Anthony Kennedy voted with the majority 84 times more than with the minority. He is a potential swing vote.

  5. The third singular vector $\kvecuthree$ effectively records his vote and not the votes of the other justices. This lends support to the claim that Anthony Kennedy is a second, somewhat less influential, swing vote.

exercises.prompt:
Suppose that $\kA=\kUr\kSigmar\kVr^T$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of the $m\times n$ matrix $\kA$. The matrix $\kAplus = \kVr\kSigmarinv\kUr^T$ is called the Moore-Penrose inverse of $\kA$.

  1. Explain why $\kAplus$ is an $n\times m$ matrix.

  2. If $\kA$ is an invertible, square matrix, explain why $\kAplus=\kAinv$.

  3. Explain why $\kA\kAplus\kvecb=\kvecbhat$, the orthogonal projection of $\kvecb$ onto $\kCol(\kA)$.

  4. Explain why $\kAplus\kA\kvecx=\kvecxhat$, the orthogonal projection of $\kvecx$ onto $\kCol(\kAT)$.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. Find the number of columns of $\kUr^T$ and the number of rows of $\kVr$.

  2. If $\kA$ is invertible, then $\kA$ is an $m\times m$ matrix whose rank is $m$.

  3. $\kA\kAplus = (\kUr\kSigmar\kVr^T)(\kVr\kSigmainv\kUr^T) = \kUr\kUr^T$

  4. $\kA\kAplus = (\kVr\kSigmainv\kUr^T)(\kUr\kSigmar\kVr^T) \kVr\kVr^T$

Solution.

  1. The number of columns of $\kAplus$ is the number of columns of $\kUr^T$, which is $m$, and the number of rows is the number of rows of $\kVr$, which is $n$.

  2. If $\kA$ is invertible, then $\kA$ is an $m\times m$ matrix whose rank is $m$. The reduced singular value decomposition is therefore $\kA=\kU\kSigma \kVT$ so that $\kAplus=\kV\kSigmainv\kUT = (\kU\kSigma \kVT)^{-1}=\kAinv$.

  3. $\kA\kAplus = (\kUr\kSigmar\kVr^T)(\kVr\kSigmainv\kUr^T) = \kUr\kUr^T$, which projects vectors orthogonal onto $\kCol(\kA)$ since the columns of $\kUr$ are an orthonormal basis for $\kCol(\kA)$.

  4. $\kA\kAplus = (\kVr\kSigmainv\kUr^T)(\kUr\kSigmar\kVr^T) \kVr\kVr^T$, which projects vectors orthogonal onto $\kCol(\kAT)$ since the columns of $\kVr$ are an orthonormal basis for $\kCol(\kAT)$.

exercises.prompt:
In Subsection 5.1.2, we saw how some linear algebraic computations are sensitive to round off error made by a computer. A singular value decomposition can help us understand when this situation can occur. For instance, consider the matrices

$$ \kA = \begin{bmatrix} 1.0001 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix},\hspace{24pt} \kB = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix}. $$

The entries in these matrices are quite close to one another, but $\kA$ is invertible while $\kB$ is not. It seems like $\kA$ is almost singular. In fact, we can measure how close a matrix is to being singular by forming the condition number, $\ksigmaone/\ksigman$, the ratio of the largest to smallest singular value. If $\kA$ were singular, the condition number would be undefined because the singular value $\ksigman=0$. Therefore, we will think of matrices with large condition numbers as being close to singular.

  1. Define the matrix $\kA$ and find a singular value decomposition. What is the condition number of $\kA$?

  2. Define the left singular vectors $\kvecuone$ and $\kvecutwo$. Compare the results $\kAinv\kvecb$ when

    1. $\kvecb=\kvecuone+\kvecutwo$.

    2. $\kvecb=2\kvecuone+\kvecutwo$.

    Notice how a small change in the vector $\kvecb$ leads to a small change in $\kAinv\kvecb$.

  3. Now compare the results $\kAinv\kvecb$ when

    1. $\kvecb=\kvecuone+\kvecutwo$.

    2. $\kvecb=\kvecuone+2\kvecutwo$.

    Notice now how a small change in $\kvecb$ leads to a large change in $\kAinv\kvecb$.

  4. Previously, we saw that, if we write $\kvecx$ in terms of left singular vectors $\kvecx=c_1\kvecvone+c_2\kvecvtwo$, then we have

    $$ \kvecb=\kA\kvecx = c_1\ksigmaone\kvecuone + c_2\ksigmatwo\kvecutwo. $$

    If we write $\kvecb=d_1\kvecuone+d_2\kvecutwo$, explain why $\kAinv\kvecb$ is sensitive to small changes in $d_2$.

Generally speaking, a square matrix $\kA$ with a large condition number will demonstrate this type of behavior so that the computation of $\kAinv$ is likely to be affected by round off error. We call such a matrix ill-conditioned.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. The condition number is $40,000$

    1. $\kAinv\kvecb = \left[\begin{array}{r}-14142.5 \\ 14142.5 \end{array}\right]$

    2. $\kAinv\kvecb = \left[\begin{array}{r}-14142.8 \\ 14142.8 \end{array}\right]$

    1. $\kAinv\kvecb = \left[\begin{array}{r}-14142.5 \\ 14142.5 \end{array}\right]$

    2. $\kAinv\kvecb = \left[\begin{array}{r}-28284.6 \\ 28285.3 \end{array}\right]$

  4. $c_2=\frac{d_2}{\ksigmatwo}$

Solution.

  1. The singular values of $\kA$ are $2$ and $5\times10^{-5}$, which means the condition number is $40,000$.

    1. $\kAinv\kvecb = \left[\begin{array}{r}-14142.5 \\ 14142.5 \end{array}\right]$

    2. $\kAinv\kvecb = \left[\begin{array}{r}-14142.8 \\ 14142.8 \end{array}\right]$

    1. $\kAinv\kvecb = \left[\begin{array}{r}-14142.5 \\ 14142.5 \end{array}\right]$

    2. $\kAinv\kvecb = \left[\begin{array}{r}-28284.6 \\ 28285.3 \end{array}\right]$

  4. We have $d_i = \ksigmai c_i$ so $c_i=\frac{d_i}{\ksigmai}$. Since $\ksigmatwo$ is so much smaller than $\ksigmaone$, even small changes in $d_2$ can lead to relatively large changes in $c_2$.

footnotes.html: The answer to part f prints $\kVr^T\kVr = \kI$; the part asks for the product $\kVr\kVr^T$, which is $\kI$ too here, since $\kVr = \kV$ is square, as the solution says.
The solution to part d prints $\kUtwo(\kU\kSigma \kVT)$; the product meant is $\kUtwo^T\kA = \kUtwo^T(\kU\kSigma \kVT)$, as the line begins.

The answer and the solution to part d print $\kA\kAplus = (\kVr\kSigmainv\kUr^T)(\kUr\kSigmar\kVr^T) \kVr\kVr^T$; the product meant is $\kAplus\kA = (\kVr\kSigmarinv\kUr^T)(\kUr\kSigmar\kVr^T) = \kVr\kVr^T$.
The vectors $\kvecvone$ and $\kvecvtwo$ in $\kvecx = c_1\kvecvone + c_2\kvecvtwo$ are the right singular vectors of $\kA$, not the left ones.

The answer and the solution to part b ii print $\kAinv\kvecb = \left[\begin{array}{r}-14142.8 \\ 14142.8 \end{array}\right]$. Since $\kAinv\kvecuone = \frac{1}{\ksigmaone}\kvecvone$ has both entries about $0.35$ in size and of one sign, adding $\kvecuone$ to $\kvecb$ moves both entries of $\kAinv\kvecb$ the same way, and with the signs of part c ii the result is $\left[\begin{array}{r}-14142.8 \\ 14142.1 \end{array}\right]$; the point of the part, a small change, stands.
